title: Balak: a hired curse (Numbers 22:2–6)
hook: the king of Moab pays the prophet Balaam to curse Israel

segments.voice: Yesterday, a copper serpent on a pole, and the Mishnah's teaching that it was the looking up that healed. Your line was look up and live. Did you lift your eyes from the screen? Day four hundred sixty-one.

A glowing review of a hotel, written by someone the hotel paid. A study about sugar, funded by a sugar company. An expert on the news who turns out to work for the people he's defending. We've learned to ask a simple question before we believe what someone says: who's paying for this? The Torah asked it first. A new portion begins today, and for once the Israelites barely appear in it. The whole story happens on the other side of the hill, where a frightened king is reaching for his wallet.
screen: `A PAID REVIEW, A FUNDED STUDY.` → `WHO'S PAYING FOR THIS?` → `A FRIGHTENED KING, ACROSS THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Balak, son of Zippor, is king of Moab. He has watched Israel defeat the kings nearby, and Moab is terrified. In the text's vivid picture, paraphrased, this crowd will lick up everything around us the way an ox licks up the grass of the field. So Balak doesn't raise an army. He hires a curse. He sends messengers to a famous seer named Balaam, son of Beor, who lives far off by the River, with a request: come and curse this people for me. And then the flattery that sounds like a sales pitch. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed." The elders set out with the fees for divination in their hands. Payment up front. Two surprises here. First, Balaam may not be only a character in a story. In 1967, archaeologists working at a site called Deir Alla, in Jordan, found an ancient plaster inscription that speaks of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods. Scholars date it to around the eighth century before the common era. So a seer by that name was remembered outside the Bible too. Second, the rabbis read Balaam as someone whose gift was for sale. In Pirkei Avot, they contrast the students of Abraham, who have a generous eye, a humble spirit and a modest appetite, with the students of Balaam, who have a grudging eye, a proud spirit and a greedy appetite. And notice the portion's name. It isn't called Balaam, after the prophet. It's called Balak, after the man with the money.
screen: `BALAK: A KING AFRAID.` · `HE WHOM THOU CURSEST IS CURSED.` · `DEIR ALLA: BALAAM IN PLASTER.` · `NAMED FOR THE MAN WITH THE MONEY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who's paying for an opinion. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one opinion you picked up recently: about a product, a person, a piece of news, maybe even about yourself. Trace it back. Where did it come from? Did someone gain anything by your believing it? There's no need to be cynical; many opinions are honest. Just look for the hand on the wallet, if there is one. Then let the question go, and simply breathe until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Balak. The king of Moab who tried to buy a curse, and the name of the portion that tells the story of the prophet he hired.
Your line: who's paying. Today, when an ad, a post or a pitch tries to change your mind, ask that question once before you agree. Day four hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The portion of Balak is read in synagogue in early summer; it's one of the few Torah stories told almost entirely from outside the camp of Israel.

fork.setup: you're a frightened king. a huge people is camped near your border. what's your plan?
options: pay a famous seer to curse them.
fork.reveal: Balak sends for Balaam with the fees for divination in hand: for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed.

original.note: Hebrew: Balak, son of Zippor, king of Moab, whose name the portion takes.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king and a wizard in an old story.
what it means: a king tries to buy a curse, and the portion is named for the one paying.
what a scholar hears: the Deir Alla plaster inscription (found 1967) names 'Balaam son of Beor', and Avot 5:19 makes him the type of the grudging eye, proud spirit and greedy appetite.

notes: Numbers 22:6 JPS 1917: 'for I know that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed.' Confirm.
Numbers 22:4 (ox licking up grass) and 22:7 (rewards of divination) paraphrased.
Deir Alla: discovered 1967 (by a Dutch team), plaster inscription naming Balaam son of Beor; dated roughly ninth to eighth century BCE. Confirm dating.
Avot 5:19 numbering varies by edition (5:22 in some); confirm the three traits as paraphrased.
